questions.questionText: What is Git?

options.text: A cloud-based code hosting platform
A distributed version control system that tracks changes to files over time
A programming language for automation scripts
A project management tool for software teams

explanation.correct: Git is a distributed version control system (DVCS) created by Linus Torvalds in 2005. It tracks changes to files, allows multiple people to collaborate, and maintains a full history of every change.
explanation.incorrect: GitHub is the cloud-based hosting platform. Git is the underlying tool that works locally and remotely.
explanation.examTip: Git = the tool (local). GitHub = the hosting platform (cloud). You can use Git without GitHub, but GitHub requires Git.

questions.questionText: What is the difference between Git and GitHub?

options.text: They are the same tool with different names
Git is the version control system; GitHub is a cloud-based platform that hosts Git repositories and adds collaboration features
GitHub is the command-line tool; Git is the web interface
Git is owned by Microsoft; GitHub is owned by the open source community

explanation.correct: Git is the open-source version control system that runs locally. GitHub is a cloud platform (owned by Microsoft) that hosts Git repositories and adds features like pull requests, issues, Actions, and Codespaces.
explanation.incorrect: GitHub is owned by Microsoft (acquired 2018). Git is maintained by the open source community.
explanation.examTip: Git = VCS tool. GitHub = hosting platform with collaboration features. Other Git hosts: GitLab, Bitbucket, Azure Repos.

questions.questionText: What does `git init` do?

options.text: Downloads a remote repository to your local machine
Initialises a new Git repository in the current directory
Pushes local changes to a remote repository
Lists all branches in the repository

explanation.correct: `git init` creates a new empty Git repository in the current directory by adding a hidden `.git` folder that stores all version control metadata.
explanation.incorrect: `git clone` downloads a remote repo. `git push` uploads changes. `git branch` lists branches.
explanation.examTip: git init = start a new repo locally. git clone = copy an existing remote repo. Two ways to start working with Git.

questions.questionText: What is the purpose of `git clone`?

options.text: Creates a copy of a remote repository on your local machine
Creates a duplicate branch from the current branch
Copies files from one directory to another
Merges two branches together

explanation.correct: `git clone <url>` copies a remote repository (including its full history) to your local machine, setting up a connection to the remote as `origin`.
explanation.incorrect: Branch duplication = `git branch`. File copying is OS commands. Merging = `git merge`.
explanation.examTip: git clone copies the entire repository history, not just current files. Sets up `origin` remote automatically.

questions.questionText: Place the steps of the basic Git workflow in the correct order.

orderItems.text: Edit files in the working directory

explanation.correct: Git workflow: Edit â†’ Stage (add) â†’ Commit â†’ Push. The staging area allows you to craft commits carefully before saving them.
explanation.incorrect: You must stage before committing. Committing saves locally. Pushing uploads to remote.
explanation.examTip: Git areas: Working Directory â†’ Staging Area (index) â†’ Local Repository â†’ Remote Repository. Each step moves changes forward.

questions.questionText: What does `git commit -m "message"` do?

options.text: Uploads staged changes to GitHub
Saves staged changes to the local repository history with a descriptive message
Adds all changed files to the staging area
Creates a new branch with the given message as its name

explanation.correct: `git commit` saves the staged changes as a snapshot in the local repository history. The `-m` flag provides a commit message describing what changed.
explanation.incorrect: Uploading = `git push`. Staging all = `git add .`. Creating branch = `git branch` or `git checkout -b`.
explanation.examTip: Commits are local until pushed. Good commit messages: present tense, descriptive, explain WHY not just WHAT.

questions.questionText: What is the difference between `git fetch` and `git pull`?

options.text: They are identical commands
`git fetch` downloads changes from remote without merging; `git pull` fetches AND merges into the current branch
`git pull` downloads files; `git fetch` downloads commits only
`git fetch` works offline; `git pull` requires internet

explanation.correct: `git fetch` downloads remote changes to your local repo but doesn't modify your working files. `git pull` = `git fetch` + `git merge` â€” downloads and integrates changes.
explanation.incorrect: Both require internet. Both download commits. The key difference is whether changes are merged into the working branch.
explanation.examTip: Fetch = safe preview (see what changed). Pull = fetch + merge (update your branch). Use fetch first when unsure about incoming changes.

questions.questionText: What is a commit hash in Git?

options.text: A password used to authenticate with GitHub
A unique identifier (SHA-1 checksum) that uniquely identifies each commit
A compressed archive of the repository files
A tag applied to mark a specific release

explanation.correct: Every Git commit is identified by a 40-character SHA-1 hash (e.g., `a3f2bc1...`) that is computed from the commit content. This guarantees integrity â€” any change produces a different hash.
explanation.incorrect: GitHub authentication uses tokens/SSH keys. Compressed archives are different. Tags are human-readable labels that can point to commits.
explanation.examTip: You can reference commits by their full hash or the first 7 characters (short hash). Git uses SHA-1 (transitioning to SHA-256) for content-addressable storage.

questions.questionText: What is the purpose of a `.gitignore` file?

options.text: Specifies files and patterns that Git should not track or commit
Lists contributors who should be ignored in pull request reviews
Hides files from the GitHub web interface
Prevents specific branches from being pushed

explanation.correct: `.gitignore` contains patterns for files and directories that Git should not track â€” like build artifacts, `node_modules/`, `.env` files with secrets, IDE settings, and OS files like `.DS_Store`.
explanation.incorrect: `.gitignore` is about file tracking, not contributors, UI visibility, or branch protection.
explanation.examTip: Common .gitignore entries: `node_modules/`, `*.log`, `.env`, `dist/`, `.DS_Store`. GitHub provides language-specific .gitignore templates.

questions.questionText: What does `git stash` do?

options.text: Permanently deletes uncommitted changes
Temporarily saves uncommitted changes so you can work on something else and restore them later
Moves commits from one branch to another
Archives old branches for long-term storage

explanation.correct: `git stash` saves uncommitted changes (both staged and unstaged) to a temporary stack, cleaning your working directory. `git stash pop` restores the most recent stash.
explanation.incorrect: Stash is temporary and reversible â€” not deletion. Moving commits = `git cherry-pick` or `git rebase`. Archiving is a different concept.
explanation.examTip: git stash use case: you're mid-feature and need to urgently fix a bug. Stash your changes, fix the bug, then pop the stash to continue.

questions.questionText: For each statement, indicate whether it correctly describes Git concepts.

statements.text: Git stores snapshots of the entire project, not just differences between files.
`git add .` stages all changed files in the current directory.
A Git tag always points to the latest commit on a branch.
Every commit in Git contains a reference to its parent commit(s).

explanation.correct: Git snapshots entire state. `git add .` stages all changes. Every commit has a parent (forming the history chain). Tags point to specific commits, not necessarily the latest.
explanation.incorrect: Tags point to a specific fixed commit (like v1.0.0), not the moving tip of a branch. Branches point to the latest commit.
explanation.examTip: Tag = fixed pointer to a specific commit (like a release marker). Branch = moving pointer that advances with each new commit.

questions.questionText: What is a remote in Git?

options.text: A branch that is stored only on your local machine
A reference to a repository hosted on a server (like GitHub) that you can push to and pull from
A Git command for working with files remotely
A backup copy of the repository stored locally

explanation.correct: A remote is a named reference to a repository hosted elsewhere (GitHub, GitLab, etc.). `origin` is the conventional name for the primary remote set up by `git clone`.
explanation.incorrect: Remotes point to external servers, not local machines. `git remote` is a command but 'remote' itself is the concept.
explanation.examTip: Common remote commands: `git remote -v` (list remotes), `git remote add origin <url>` (add remote), `git push origin main` (push to remote branch).

questions.questionText: Match each Git command to its correct purpose.

dropdowns.prompt: Download remote changes and merge into current branch
Upload local commits to a remote repository
Download remote changes without modifying working files

explanation.correct: git pull = fetch + merge. git push = upload local commits. git fetch = download metadata only (no merge). git clone = initial copy of entire repo.
explanation.incorrect: These four commands are the core remote operations. Know the difference between fetch and pull.
explanation.examTip: Remote operations: clone (first time), fetch (see what changed), pull (fetch+merge), push (upload). Most common: pull then push.

questions.questionText: What is `HEAD` in Git?

options.text: The first commit ever made in the repository
A pointer indicating the current position in the repository â€” usually the tip of the current branch
The main or default branch of a repository
A special tag applied to the most recent commit

explanation.correct: HEAD is a symbolic reference pointing to the current branch (and the latest commit on that branch). A 'detached HEAD' occurs when you check out a specific commit rather than a branch.
explanation.incorrect: HEAD is not the first commit, the main branch itself, or a tag. It points to where you currently are.
explanation.examTip: HEAD = where you are now. Usually HEAD â†’ branch â†’ latest commit. Detached HEAD = HEAD â†’ specific commit hash.

questions.questionText: What does `git log` show?

options.text: Files changed in the working directory
The commit history including hashes, authors, dates, and messages
All active branches in the repository
A log of Git errors and warnings

explanation.correct: `git log` displays the commit history. Use flags: `--oneline` (condensed), `--graph` (visual), `--author` (filter).
explanation.incorrect: Changed files = `git status`. Branches = `git branch`.
explanation.examTip: `git log --oneline --graph` shows a visual branch history. `git log --since='2 weeks ago'` filters by time.

questions.questionText: What does `git status` show?

options.text: The most recent commit hash and message
The current branch, staged files, unstaged changes, and untracked files
The connection status to the remote repository
The list of active branches

explanation.correct: `git status` shows the working tree state: current branch, staged files, modified unstaged files, and untracked files.
explanation.incorrect: Last commit = `git log -1`. Remote = `git remote -v`. Branches = `git branch`.
explanation.examTip: Run `git status` frequently â€” it's read-only and tells you exactly what to do next.

questions.questionText: What is the difference between `git reset` and `git revert`?

options.text: They are identical â€” both undo the last commit
`git reset` rewrites history; `git revert` creates a new commit undoing changes, preserving history
`git revert` only works on staged changes; `git reset` on committed changes
`git reset` works on remote branches; `git revert` on local only

explanation.correct: `git reset` moves the branch pointer backwards rewriting history â€” dangerous on shared branches. `git revert` creates a new commit inverting the target commit â€” safe on shared branches.
explanation.incorrect: They are fundamentally different. Revert is safe for shared branches.
explanation.examTip: Shared branch? Use `git revert`. Local-only? Can use `git reset`. Never rewrite pushed commits others depend on.

questions.questionText: What is a merge conflict in Git?

options.text: An error that prevents pushing to a remote branch
A situation where two branches made conflicting changes to the same part of a file that Git cannot automatically resolve
A failed merge of a deleted branch
A permission error when merging a protected branch

explanation.correct: Merge conflicts occur when two branches modify the same lines differently. Git marks conflicting sections with `<<<<<<<`, `=======`, `>>>>>>>` markers for manual resolution.
explanation.incorrect: Push errors are different. Deleted branch merges fail differently. Permission errors = branch protection.
explanation.examTip: Resolve conflicts: open file, choose changes, remove markers, `git add`, `git commit`. Use a visual merge tool for complex conflicts.

questions.questionText: What is the difference between SSH and HTTPS authentication for GitHub?

options.text: HTTPS is more secure; SSH is only for advanced users
SSH uses key-based authentication (no password after setup); HTTPS uses username/token credentials
SSH only works on Linux
HTTPS supports pushing; SSH only supports pulling

explanation.correct: SSH uses public/private key pairs â€” no password needed after setup. HTTPS uses username + personal access token. Both are secure and support push/pull.
explanation.incorrect: SSH works on all platforms. Both support push and pull. Both are secure.
explanation.examTip: SSH setup: `ssh-keygen` â†’ add public key to GitHub Settings â†’ SSH Keys. HTTPS: use a PAT (passwords removed Aug 2021).

questions.questionText: What is `git cherry-pick`?

options.text: Selects which files to include in a commit
Applies changes from a specific commit onto the current branch without merging the entire branch
Selects the best merge strategy automatically
Filters commits by author

explanation.correct: `git cherry-pick <hash>` takes a specific commit and applies its changes to the current branch â€” useful for backporting a bug fix to a release branch.
explanation.incorrect: File selection = `git add -p`. Auto merge strategy = Git internals. Author filtering = `git log --author`.
explanation.examTip: Cherry-pick: apply a hotfix to multiple release branches, backport a specific feature. Creates a new commit with a different hash.

questions.scenarioText: A developer accidentally committed sensitive API keys to a public repository and pushed to GitHub.
questions.questionText: What are the MOST important immediate steps?

options.text: Delete the commit using `git reset` and force push
Immediately revoke and rotate the exposed credentials, then clean the repository history
Make the repository private temporarily
Delete the entire repository and recreate it

explanation.correct: Assume credentials were already scraped. First: revoke/rotate immediately. Then clean history using `git filter-repo` or BFG Repo Cleaner.
explanation.incorrect: Making private doesn't protect already-exposed credentials. Deleting the repo loses all history.
explanation.examTip: Exposed secret response: 1) Revoke. 2) Rotate. 3) Clean history. 4) Add to .gitignore. 5) Add pre-commit hooks to prevent recurrence.

questions.questionText: Place the steps of the GitHub open source contribution workflow in the correct order.

orderItems.text: Fork the upstream repository to your GitHub account
Create a feature branch and make changes
Push branch to your fork on GitHub
Open a pull request from your fork to the upstream repository

explanation.correct: Open source workflow: Fork â†’ Clone â†’ Branch & Change â†’ Push to fork â†’ PR to upstream. This is the standard contribution pattern.
explanation.incorrect: You must fork before cloning. Push before PR. PR is the final step to propose changes.
explanation.examTip: This is the GitHub Flow for open source: Fork + Clone + Branch + Push + PR. For internal projects: just Branch + Push + PR (no fork needed).

questions.questionText: What is `git diff` used for?

options.text: Shows the commit history of the repository
Shows the differences between the working directory, staging area, or commits
Displays which branches differ from main
Identifies merge conflicts in a file

explanation.correct: `git diff` shows line-by-line differences. `git diff` = unstaged changes. `git diff --staged` = staged changes. `git diff branch1 branch2` = between branches.
explanation.incorrect: History = `git log`. Branch differences = `git diff branch1 branch2`. Conflicts = shown in file content after failed merge.
explanation.examTip: git diff variants: `git diff` (working vs staged), `git diff --staged` (staged vs last commit), `git diff HEAD` (all changes vs last commit), `git diff hash1 hash2`.

questions.questionText: What does `git branch -d feature-branch` do?

options.text: Deletes the branch from the remote repository
Deletes the local branch if its changes have been merged
Disables the branch from receiving new commits
Detaches HEAD from the branch

explanation.correct: `git branch -d` deletes a local branch safely â€” it fails if the branch has unmerged changes. Use `-D` (force) to delete regardless. To delete remote: `git push origin --delete feature-branch`.
explanation.incorrect: Remote deletion needs `git push origin --delete`. `-d` doesn't disable or detach.
explanation.examTip: Branch cleanup: `git branch -d branch` (safe local delete), `git push origin --delete branch` (remote delete). GitHub can auto-delete branches after PR merge.

questions.questionText: What is `git rebase -i` (interactive rebase) used for?

options.text: Rebasing between two remote repositories interactively
Rewriting, squashing, reordering, or editing commits in a branch's history before sharing
Interactively resolving merge conflicts one file at a time
Reviewing code changes interactively before committing

explanation.correct: Interactive rebase opens an editor showing commits you can reword, squash (combine), fixup, drop, or reorder â€” letting you clean up a messy local history before sharing a well-organised set of commits.
explanation.incorrect: Interactive rebase is for local history editing, not remote-to-remote rebase, conflict resolution, or pre-commit review.
explanation.examTip: Interactive rebase commands: pick (keep), reword (edit message), squash (combine with previous), fixup (squash, discard message), drop (remove). Use before pushing.

questions.questionText: What is the GitHub Flow branching strategy?

options.text: A strategy with main, develop, feature, release, and hotfix branches
A simple workflow: branch from main, commit, open PR, review, merge to main, deploy
A strategy where all developers commit directly to main without branches
A workflow using tags instead of branches for release management

explanation.correct: GitHub Flow is a lightweight branching strategy: create a branch from main â†’ commit changes â†’ open PR â†’ review â†’ merge to main â†’ deploy. Main is always deployable.
explanation.incorrect: main + develop + feature + release + hotfix = Git Flow (more complex). Direct commits to main = trunk-based development. Tags are for versioning, not flow.
explanation.examTip: GitHub Flow: simple, continuous delivery. main = always deployable. Branch â†’ PR â†’ merge â†’ deploy. Suitable for small teams and continuous deployment environments.
